name: Chapter 3: Matrices
description: Order and types of matrices, equality, addition and scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication, transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, invertible matrices, and exam-style problems.

cards.term: Define a matrix.
cards.definition: An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. The numbers are its elements (entries); horizontal lines are rows, vertical lines are columns

cards.term: What is the order of a matrix? How many elements?
cards.definition: m rows and n columns: order m × n (“m by n”), with mn elements. Rows come first, then columns

cards.term: What does aᵢⱼ mean?
cards.definition: The element in the i-th row and j-th column. So the i-th row is (aᵢ₁, ..., aᵢₙ) and the j-th column is (a₁ⱼ, ..., aₘⱼ)

cards.term: Example 2: if a matrix has 8 elements, what orders are possible?
cards.definition: All pairs of natural numbers with product 8: 1 × 8, 8 × 1, 2 × 4, 4 × 2

cards.term: How do you find all possible orders for a matrix with N elements?
cards.definition: List the ordered factor pairs (m, n) with mn = N. A prime N (like 13 or 5) gives only 1 × N and N × 1

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q1: for A = [[2, 5, 19, −7], [35, −2, 5/2, 12], [√3, 1, −5, 17]] find the order, number of elements, a₁₃, a₂₁, a₃₃, a₂₄, a₂₃.
cards.definition: Order 3 × 4, 12 elements. a₁₃ = 19, a₂₁ = 35, a₃₃ = −5, a₂₄ = 12, a₂₃ = 5/2

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q2: possible orders for 24 elements? for 13 elements?
Ex 3.1 Q3: possible orders for 18 elements? for 5 elements?
Ex 3.1 Q4(i): build the 2 × 2 matrix with aᵢⱼ = (i + j)²/2.
cards.definition: a₁₁ = 2, a₁₂ = 9/2, a₂₁ = 9/2, a₂₂ = 8: [[2, 9/2], [9/2, 8]]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q4(ii),(iii): 2 × 2 with aᵢⱼ = i/j, and with aᵢⱼ = (i + 2j)²/2.
cards.definition: (ii) [[1, 1/2], [2, 1]]. (iii) a₁₁ = 9/2, a₁₂ = 25/2, a₂₁ = 8, a₂₂ = 18: [[9/2, 25/2], [8, 18]]

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q5: build the 3 × 4 matrices with (i) aᵢⱼ = ½|−3i + j| and (ii) aᵢⱼ = 2i − j.
How are the vertices of a polygon written as a matrix?
cards.definition: Each vertex (x, y) is a row [x y] (or a column). ABCD with A(1,0), B(3,2), C(1,3), D(−1,2) is a 4 × 2 matrix with rows [1 0], [3 2], [1 3], [−1 2]. Transformations (rotation, reflection) are then matrix multiplications

cards.term: Types of matrices
cards.definition: Column matrix: only one column (m × 1); Row matrix: only one row (1 × n); Square matrix: rows = columns (n × n); diagonal a₁₁, a₂₂, …, aₙₙ; Diagonal matrix: square, aᵢⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j; Scalar matrix: diagonal with all diagonal entries equal (k); Identity matrix Iₙ: diagonal with all diagonal entries 1; Zero matrix O: all elements 0 (any order)

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Types of matrices

Define each type of matrix.

Column matrixonly one column (m × 1)
Row matrixonly one row (1 × n)
Square matrixrows = columns (n × n); diagonal a₁₁, a₂₂, …, aₙₙ
Diagonal matrixsquare, aᵢⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j
Scalar matrixdiagonal with all diagonal entries equal (k)
Identity matrix Iₙdiagonal with all diagonal entries 1
Zero matrix Oall elements 0 (any order)

Identity ⊂ scalar ⊂ diagonal ⊂ square

cards.term: How are identity, scalar and diagonal matrices related?
cards.definition: Identity ⊂ scalar ⊂ diagonal ⊂ square. Every identity matrix is scalar (k = 1), every scalar matrix is diagonal, but a diagonal matrix like diag(1, 2) is not scalar

cards.term: Is a zero matrix a square matrix? Is it a diagonal matrix?
cards.definition: A zero matrix can have any order. If it is square it is also diagonal and scalar (k = 0), but not an identity matrix

cards.term: Define equal matrices.
cards.definition: Same order and aᵢⱼ = bᵢⱼ for every position. [[2, 3], [0, 1]] ≠ [[2, 3, 0]] because the orders differ

cards.term: Example 4: two equal 3 × 3 matrices give x + 3 = 0, z + 4 = 6, 2y − 7 = 3y − 2, a − 1 = −3, 0 = 2c + 2, b − 3 = 2b + 4. Solve.
cards.definition: Each equation has one unknown: x = −3, z = 2, y = −5, a = −2, c = −1, b = −7
Two systems: 2a + b = 4, a − 2b = −3 give a = 1, b = 2; 5c − d = 11, 4c + 3d = 24 give c = 3, d = 4
Equal entries: y = 4, z = 3, x = 1
z = 0, x + y = 6, xy = 8: x, y are 2 and 4 in either order: (x, y, z) = (2, 4, 0) or (4, 2, 0)

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q6(iii): column (x + y + z, x + z, y + z) = (9, 5, 7).
cards.definition: Subtract: y = 9 − 5 = 4, x = 9 − 7 = 2, z = 3: x = 2, y = 4, z = 3
a − b = −1 and 2a − b = 0 give a = 1, b = 2. Then 2 + c = 5 gives c = 3; 9 + d = 13 gives d = 4: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q8: A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ is a square matrix if (A) m < n (B) m > n (C) m = n (D) none
cards.definition: (C) m = n

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q9: for which x, y are [[3x + 7, 5], [y + 1, 2 − 3x]] and [[0, y − 2], [8, 4]] equal?
cards.definition: x = −7/3 and y = 7 from the first row and first column, but then 2 − 3x = 9 ≠ 4. Not possible (B)

cards.term: Ex 3.1 Q10: number of 3 × 3 matrices with each entry 0 or 1?
cards.definition: Nine entries, two choices each: 2⁹ = 512 (D)

cards.term: When can two matrices be added? How?
cards.definition: Only when they have the same order. Add corresponding entries: (A + B)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ

cards.term: Multiplication of a matrix by a scalar k?
cards.definition: kA = [k aᵢⱼ]: multiply every element by k. −A = (−1)A, and A − B = A + (−1)B (same order needed)

cards.term: Properties of matrix addition?
cards.definition: Commutative A + B = B + A; associative (A + B) + C = A + (B + C); additive identity O (A + O = A); additive inverse −A (A + (−A) = O)

cards.term: Properties of scalar multiplication?
cards.definition: k(A + B) = kA + kB and (k + l)A = kA + lA (also k(lA) = (kl)A and 1·A = A)

cards.term: Method: solve 2A + 3X = 5B for X.
cards.definition: 3X = 5B − 2A, so X = (1/3)(5B − 2A). Treat matrix equations like algebra but never divide by a matrix; multiply by scalars only

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q2(i),(ii): [[a, b], [−b, a]] + [[a, b], [b, a]] and [[a² + b², b² + c²], [a² + c², a² + b²]] + [[2ab, 2bc], [−2ac, −2ab]].
cards.definition: (i) [[2a, 2b], [0, 2a]]. (ii) [[(a + b)², (b + c)²], [(a − c)², (a − b)²]]
(iii) [[11, 11, 0], [16, 5, 21], [5, 10, 9]]. (iv) [[cos²x + sin²x, sin²x + cos²x], [same, same]] = [[1, 1], [1, 1]]
A + B = [[4, 1, −1], [9, 2, 7], [3, −1, 4]], B − C = [[−1, −2, 0], [4, −1, 3], [1, 2, 0]]. Then A + (B − C) = (A + B) − C by associativity
Each entry: 3aᵢⱼ − 5bᵢⱼ = 0 (for example 3·2/3 − 5·2/5 = 0): the 3 × 3 zero matrix

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q6: simplify cos θ [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] + sin θ [[sin θ, −cos θ], [cos θ, sin θ]].
cards.definition: Top-left cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, top-right cosθ sinθ − sinθ cosθ = 0, and so on: I = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
X = ½(sum + difference) = [[5, 0], [1, 4]], Y = ½(sum − difference) = [[2, 0], [1, 1]]

Eliminate: X = (3Q − 2P)/5 and Y = (3P − 2Q)/5 where P, Q are the two right-hand sides. That gives X = [[2/5, −12/5], [−11/5, 3]] and Y = [[2/5, 13/5], [14/5, −2]]. Check: 2X + 3Y top-left = 4/5 + 6/5 = 2 ✓
LHS = [[2 + y, 6], [1, 2x + 2]]. So y = 3 and 2x + 2 = 8: x = 3, y = 3
2x − y = 10 and 3x + y = 5. Add: 5x = 15: x = 3, y = −4
3x = x + 4, 3y = 6 + x + y, 3z = −1 + z + w, 3w = 2w + 3: x = 2, y = 4, w = 3, z = 1

cards.term: When is the product AB defined, and what is its order?
cards.definition: When columns of A = rows of B. For A (m × n) and B (n × p): AB is m × p

cards.term: Order of a matrix product: inner numbers match, outer numbers remain
cards.definition: (m x n)(n x p) = (m x p): number of columns of A must equal number of rows of B; AB may exist while BA does not

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Matrix multiplication · orders

A has order 2 × 3 and B has order 3 × 4. Is AB defined? Is BA? What is the order of the product?

Compare the columns of A with the rows of B.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Matrix multiplication · orders

A has order 2 × 3 and B has order 3 × 4. Is AB defined? Is BA? What is the order of the product?

(m × n)(n × p) = (m × p): the inner numbers must match; the outer numbers give the order.

AB is 2 × 4. BA would need 4 = 2, so BA is not defined. Both AB and BA exist only if A is m × n and B is n × m; then AB is m × m and BA is n × n.

cards.term: Matrix product: row of A times column of B
cards.definition: Entry (i,j) of AB = sum over k of a_ik b_kj (row i of A dot column j of B); AB for A=[[2,4],[3,2]], B=[[1,3],[-2,5]] is [[-6,26],[-1,19]]

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Matrix multiplication · row × column

Multiply A = [[2, 4], [3, 2]] and B = [[1, 3], [−2, 5]]. How is each entry of AB built?

Walk along a row of A and down a column of B.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Matrix multiplication · row × column

Multiply A = [[2, 4], [3, 2]] and B = [[1, 3], [−2, 5]]. How is each entry of AB built?

The (i, j) entry of AB is row i of A times column j of B, multiplied term by term and added: cᵢⱼ = Σ aᵢₖ bₖⱼ.

AB = [[2·1 + 4(−2), 2·3 + 4·5], [3·1 + 2(−2), 3·3 + 2·5]] = [[−6, 26], [−1, 19]] (Ex 3.2 Q1(iv)). Note BA = [[11, 10], [11, 2]] is different.

cards.term: Formula for the (i, k) entry of AB?
cards.definition: cᵢₖ = aᵢ₁b₁ₖ + aᵢ₂b₂ₖ + ... + aᵢₙbₙₖ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ bⱼₖ: row i of A dotted with column k of B

cards.term: Example 12: A = [[6, 9], [2, 3]], B = [[2, 6, 0], [7, 9, 8]]. Find AB. Is BA defined?
cards.definition: AB is 2 × 3: [[75, 117, 72], [25, 39, 24]]. BA: B has 3 columns but A has 2 rows: not defined

cards.term: If AB is defined, is BA defined? When are both defined?
cards.definition: Not necessarily. For A (m × n), B (k × l): both AB and BA exist iff n = k and l = m. For square matrices of the same order both always exist

cards.term: Is matrix multiplication commutative?
cards.definition: No: AB ≠ BA in general (they may even have different orders). Example 14: A = [[1, 0], [0, −1]], B = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] give AB = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] but BA = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]

cards.term: When is AB = BA guaranteed?
cards.definition: Diagonal matrices of the same order commute. Also A commutes with I, O, and any scalar matrix kI, with itself and its powers, and with polynomials in A

cards.term: Example 15: A = [[0, −1], [0, 2]], B = [[3, 5], [0, 0]]. Find AB. What does it show?
cards.definition: AB = O. So AB = O does not imply A = O or B = O (real numbers behave differently)

cards.term: Trap: does AB = AC imply B = C?
cards.definition: No (no cancellation law). A(B − C) = O does not force B = C when A ≠ O. Example: A = [[1, 1], [1, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], C = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] give AB = AC

cards.term: Properties of matrix multiplication?
cards.definition: Associative (AB)C = A(BC); distributive A(B + C) = AB + AC and (A + B)C = AC + BC; identity IA = AI = A; but not commutative

cards.term: Trap: (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B²?
cards.definition: Not in general. (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and AB ≠ BA. True only when AB = BA. Likewise (AB)² ≠ A²B² in general and A² − B² ≠ (A − B)(A + B)

cards.term: Example 19: cost per contact A = [40, 100, 50]ᵀ paise; contacts X: [1000, 500, 5000], Y: [3000, 1000, 10000]. Total cost for each city?
cards.definition: BA = X: 40 000 + 50 000 + 250 000 = 340 000 paise; Y: 120 000 + 100 000 + 500 000 = 720 000 paise, that is ₹3400 and ₹7200

A² = [[19, 4, 8], [1, 12, 8], [14, 6, 15]], A³ = [[63, 46, 69], [69, −6, 23], [92, 46, 63]]. Then A³ − 23A − 40I = O entry by entry. (Cayley–Hamilton: a matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation)
AB = [[−6, 26], [−1, 19]] and BA = [[11, 10], [11, 2]]. Different, so AB ≠ BA
Top-left a² + b², top-right −ab + ab = 0, bottom-left −ab + ab = 0, bottom-right b² + a²: (a² + b²) I

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q3(ii): the column [1, 2, 3]ᵀ times the row [2, 3, 4].
cards.definition: A 3 × 1 times a 1 × 3 gives a 3 × 3 (outer product): [[2, 3, 4], [4, 6, 8], [6, 9, 12]]

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q13: F(x) = [[cos x, −sin x, 0], [sin x, cos x, 0], [0, 0, 1]]. Show F(x)F(y) = F(x + y).
cards.definition: Top-left: cos x cos y − sin x sin y = cos(x + y); top-right: −cos x sin y − sin x cos y = −sin(x + y); and so on. Rotations about the z-axis compose by adding angles
Left: [[7, 1], [33, 34]]. Right: [[16, 5], [39, 25]]. Different

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q14(ii): the 3 × 3 non-commutativity example.
cards.definition: One order gives [[5, 8, 14], [0, −1, 1], [−1, 0, 1]], the other [[−1, −1, −3], [1, 0, 0], [6, 11, 6]]: not equal
Compute A² and A³, then combine entry by entry: every entry cancels to 0. ✓ (Cayley–Hamilton again)

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q17: A = [[3, −2], [4, −2]]. Find k with A² = kA − 2I.
cards.definition: A² = [[1, −2], [4, −4]] and kA − 2I = [[3k − 2, −2k], [4k, −2k − 2]]. Then k = 1 fits every entry: k = 1

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q18: A = [[0, −tan(α/2)], [tan(α/2), 0]]. Show I + A = (I − A)[[cos α, −sin α], [sin α, cos α]].
cards.definition: With t = tan(α/2): cos α = (1 − t²)/(1 + t²), sin α = 2t/(1 + t²). Multiply out (I − A)(rotation) = [[1, t], [−t, 1]] · [[cos α, −sin α], [sin α, cos α]] and simplify to [[1, −t], [t, 1]] = I + A. ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q19: ₹30 000 is split between bonds paying 5% and 7%. How much in each to earn (a) ₹1800 (b) ₹2000?
cards.definition: Let x and 30 000 − x: 0.05x + 0.07(30 000 − x) = interest. (a) 2100 − 0.02x = 1800 gives ₹15 000 and ₹15 000. (b) 2100 − 0.02x = 2000 gives ₹5 000 and ₹25 000

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q20: 10 dozen chemistry books at ₹80, 8 dozen physics at ₹60, 10 dozen economics at ₹40. Total receipts?
cards.definition: Quantities (120, 96, 120) times prices (80, 60, 40): 9600 + 5760 + 4800 = ₹20 160

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q21: X is 2 × n, Y is 3 × k, Z is 2 × p, W is n × 3, P is p × k. When is PY + WY defined?
cards.definition: PY = (p × k)(3 × k) needs k = 3 and then has order p × 3. WY = (n × 3)(3 × k) has order n × 3. To add them the orders must agree: p = n. (A) k = 3, p = n

cards.term: Ex 3.2 Q22: if n = p, the order of 7X − 5Z is (A) p × 2 (B) 2 × n (C) n × 3 (D) p × n
cards.definition: X is 2 × n and Z is 2 × p = 2 × n, so the combination is (B) 2 × n

cards.term: Define the transpose of a matrix.
cards.definition: A′ (or Aᵀ): swap rows and columns. If A is m × n then A′ is n × m and (A′)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ

cards.term: Properties of the transpose?
cards.definition: (A′)′ = A, (kA)′ = kA′, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (AB)′ = B′A′ (order reverses, like socks and shoes)

cards.term: Trap: (AB)′ = A′B′?
cards.definition: No. It is B′A′. A′B′ may not even be defined: A (2 × 3), B (3 × 4): AB′s transpose is 4 × 2 = (4 × 3)(3 × 2) = B′A′
(i) the row [5, 1/2, −1]. (ii) [[1, 2], [−1, 3]]. (iii) [[−1, √3, 2], [5, 5, 3], [6, 6, −1]]
AB = [[−1, 2, 1], [4, −8, −4], [−3, 6, 3]] (3 × 3); its transpose equals B′A′ = the column [−1, 2, 1]ᵀ times the row [1, −4, 3]. ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q6: A = [[cos α, sin α], [−sin α, cos α]]. Verify A′A = I.
cards.definition: A′A = [[cos²α + sin²α, 0], [0, sin²α + cos²α]] = I (A is an orthogonal / rotation matrix: A′ = A⁻¹)

cards.term: Define symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
cards.definition: Symmetric: A′ = A (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ). Skew-symmetric: A′ = −A (aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ). Both must be square

cards.term: Symmetric vs skew-symmetric: mirror in the diagonal
cards.definition: Symmetric: A^T = A, a_ij = a_ji. Skew-symmetric: A^T = -A, a_ji = -a_ij and the diagonal is zero

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Symmetric and skew-symmetric

Look at the entries of P and Q. Which one is symmetric and which is skew-symmetric? What pattern defines each?

Reflect each matrix in its main diagonal.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Symmetric and skew-symmetric

Look at the entries of P and Q. Which one is symmetric and which is skew-symmetric? What pattern defines each?

Symmetric (P′ = P): aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. Mirror the matrix in the main diagonal and nothing changes.

Skew-symmetric (Q′ = −Q): aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ. Mirrored entries are opposites, and since aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ every diagonal entry is 0.

cards.term: Why is every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix 0?
cards.definition: aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ ⇒ 2aᵢᵢ = 0 ⇒ aᵢᵢ = 0

cards.term: Theorem 1: what do you know about A + A′ and A − A′ for a square matrix A?
cards.definition: A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric ((A + A′)′ = A′ + A; (A − A′)′ = A′ − A = −(A − A′))

cards.term: Theorem 2: express any square matrix as symmetric + skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: A = ½(A + A′) + ½(A − A′). The decomposition is unique

cards.term: Can a matrix be both symmetric and skew-symmetric?
cards.definition: Only the zero matrix (A′ = A = −A ⇒ A = O). That is Misc Q10: answer (B) zero matrix
First: equals its transpose (mirror entries match: −1, 5, 1). Second: zero diagonal and mirror entries are opposites: 1 vs −1, −1 vs 1, 1 vs −1. ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q8: A = [[1, 5], [6, 7]]. Verify A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: A + A′ = [[2, 11], [11, 14]] (symmetric); A − A′ = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] (skew-symmetric). ✓

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q9: find ½(A + A′) and ½(A − A′) for A = [[0, a, b], [−a, 0, c], [−b, −c, 0]].
cards.definition: A is already skew-symmetric: ½(A + A′) = O (zero matrix) and ½(A − A′) = A itself

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q10(i): write [[3, 5], [1, −1]] as symmetric + skew-symmetric.

cards.definition: It is already symmetric: symmetric part = A, skew part = O

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q11: if A, B are symmetric of the same order, AB − BA is (A) skew-symmetric (B) symmetric (C) zero (D) identity
cards.definition: (AB − BA)′ = B′A′ − A′B′ = BA − AB = −(AB − BA): (A) skew-symmetric

cards.term: Ex 3.3 Q12: A = [[cos α, −sin α], [sin α, cos α]] and A + A′ = I. Then α = ?
cards.definition: A + A′ = 2 cos α · I = I so cos α = ½: (B) π/3

cards.term: Example 24: A, B symmetric. When is AB symmetric?
cards.definition: Exactly when AB = BA. (AB)′ = B′A′ = BA, which equals AB iff they commute

cards.term: Which of A + A′, A·A′, A′A are always symmetric for a square matrix A?
cards.definition: All three. (A + A′)′ = A + A′; (AA′)′ = (A′)′A′ = AA′; (A′A)′ = A′A. But AB for two symmetric matrices is not symmetric in general

cards.term: Misc Q1: A, B symmetric, prove AB − BA is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: (AB − BA)′ = B′A′ − A′B′ = BA − AB = −(AB − BA). ✓

cards.term: Misc Q2: show B′AB is symmetric if A is symmetric and skew-symmetric if A is skew-symmetric.
cards.definition: (B′AB)′ = B′A′(B′)′ = B′A′B. If A′ = A it equals B′AB (symmetric); if A′ = −A it equals −B′AB (skew). ✓

cards.term: Define an invertible matrix and its inverse.
cards.definition: A square matrix A of order n is invertible if ∃ a square matrix B of the same order with AB = BA = I. Then B = A⁻¹

cards.term: Can a non-square matrix have an inverse?
cards.definition: No. AB and BA would need to be equal identities of the same order, which forces A and B to be square of the same order

cards.term: The book’s example: A = [[2, 3], [1, 2]] and B = [[2, −3], [−1, 2]]. Are they inverses?
cards.definition: AB = [[4 − 3, −6 + 6], [2 − 2, −3 + 4]] = I and BA = I. So B = A⁻¹

cards.term: Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
cards.definition: A^-1 = 1/(ad-bc) [[d,-b],[-c,a]]: swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal, divide by determinant; needs ad-bc != 0

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
2 × 2 inverse shortcut

Find the inverse of A = [[a, b], [c, d]] when ad − bc ≠ 0.

Swap the diagonal, flip the other two signs.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
2 × 2 inverse shortcut

Find the inverse of A = [[a, b], [c, d]] when ad − bc ≠ 0.

A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]]: swap the diagonal, negate the other two entries, divide by ad − bc.

Example (the book’s A = [[2, 3], [1, 2]]): ad − bc = 1, so A⁻¹ = [[2, −3], [−1, 2]], and AA⁻¹ = I. If ad − bc = 0 there is no inverse. (The general method uses adjoints and determinants in Chapter 4.)

cards.term: Theorem 3: is the inverse of a matrix unique?
cards.definition: Yes. If B and C are inverses, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C

cards.term: Theorem 4: (AB)⁻¹ = ?
cards.definition: B⁻¹A⁻¹: undo the last operation first. Proof: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I. Similarly (ABC)⁻¹ = C⁻¹B⁻¹A⁻¹

cards.term: Relation between transpose and inverse: (A′)⁻¹ = ?
cards.definition: (A⁻¹)′, and (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A, (kA)⁻¹ = (1/k)A⁻¹ (k ≠ 0)

cards.term: Ex 3.4 Q1: matrices A and B are inverses of each other only if (A) AB = BA (B) AB = BA = O (C) AB = O, BA = I (D) AB = BA = I
cards.definition: (D) AB = BA = I

cards.term: Which is true: AB = I ⇒ BA = I?
cards.definition: For square matrices of the same order, yes (a one-sided inverse is two-sided). This can fail for non-square matrices

cards.term: If A is invertible and AB = AC, what follows?
cards.definition: Multiply by A⁻¹: B = C. Invertibility restores the cancellation law that fails for singular matrices

cards.term: If AB = O and A is invertible, what is B?
cards.definition: B = A⁻¹(AB) = A⁻¹O = O

cards.term: Aⁿ for the rotation matrix is rotation by nθ
cards.definition: A = [[cos t, sin t],[-sin t, cos t]] rotates vectors clockwise by t; A^n = [[cos nt, sin nt],[-sin nt, cos nt]] (induction, Example 23)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Powers of a rotation matrix

A = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] with θ = 30°. What does A do to the vector v = (1, 0)? What are A² and Aⁿ?

Follow the vector after each multiplication by A.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Powers of a rotation matrix

A = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] with θ = 30°. What does A do to the vector v = (1, 0)? What are A² and Aⁿ?

A v = (cos θ, −sin θ): the vector is rotated clockwise by θ. Applying A twice rotates by 2θ, so Aⁿ = [[cos nθ, sin nθ], [−sin nθ, cos nθ]] (Example 23, proved by induction).

Check with the product formula: A·Aᵏ has entries cos θ cos kθ − sin θ sin kθ = cos (k + 1)θ and so on.

cards.term: Example 23: A = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]. Prove Aⁿ = [[cos nθ, sin nθ], [−sin nθ, cos nθ]] for n ∈ N.
cards.definition: Induction: true for n = 1. If it holds for k, A^(k+1) = A·Aᵏ has top-left cos θ cos kθ − sin θ sin kθ = cos(k + 1)θ and top-right cos θ sin kθ + sin θ cos kθ = sin(k + 1)θ, etc. ✓

cards.term: Misc Q3: A = [[0, 2y, z], [x, y, −z], [x, −y, z]] satisfies A′A = I. Find x, y, z.
cards.definition: Columns must be orthonormal: 2x² = 1, 6y² = 1, 3z² = 1 (and the cross terms vanish): x = ±1/√2, y = ±1/√6, z = ±1/√3
Middle product = [4, x, 2x]ᵀ; then 4 + 2x + 2x = 0: x = −1
Middle product = [x + 2, 9, 2x + 3]ᵀ, then x(x + 2) − 45 − (2x + 3) = x² − 48 = 0: x = ±4√3

cards.term: Misc Q7: sales matrix: market I sells x, y, z as 10 000, 2 000, 18 000; market II as 6 000, 20 000, 8 000. Unit sale prices ₹2.50, ₹1.50, ₹1.00. Revenue in each market?
cards.definition: Multiply by the price column: I: 25 000 + 3 000 + 18 000 = ₹46 000; II: 15 000 + 30 000 + 8 000 = ₹53 000

cards.term: Misc Q7(b): unit costs ₹2.00, ₹1.00, ₹0.50. Gross profit?
Misc Q9: A = [[α, β], [γ, −α]] with A² = I. Then (A) 1 + α² + βγ = 0 (B) 1 − α² + βγ = 0 (C) 1 − α² − βγ = 0 (D) 1 + α² − βγ = 0
cards.definition: A² = (α² + βγ) I, so α² + βγ = 1: (C)

cards.term: Misc Q10: if A is both symmetric and skew-symmetric, then A is (A) diagonal (B) zero matrix (C) square (D) none
cards.definition: (B) zero matrix (it is square and diagonal too, but zero is the precise answer)

cards.term: Misc Q11: A² = A, then (I + A)³ − 7A = (A) A (B) I − A (C) I (D) 3A
cards.definition: Aⁿ = A for all n ≥ 1: (I + A)³ = I + 3A + 3A² + A³ = I + 7A, so the expression is (C) I

cards.term: Idempotent, involutory and nilpotent matrices?
cards.definition: Idempotent: A² = A. Involutory: A² = I. Nilpotent: Aᵏ = O for some k. Example: [[0, 1], [0, 0]] is nilpotent (A² = O)
Compute A², A³: [[1, 2], [0, 1]], [[1, 3], [0, 1]]. Pattern (by induction): [[1, n], [0, 1]]

cards.term: Powers of a diagonal matrix diag(a, b)?
cards.definition: diag(aⁿ, bⁿ): multiply the diagonal entries separately (diagonal matrices multiply entrywise on the diagonal)

cards.term: Find A⁻¹ for A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] with the shortcut.
Number of 3 × 3 symmetric matrices with entries in {0, 1}?
cards.definition: Six free entries (diagonal 3 and above-diagonal 3): 2⁶ = 64

cards.term: Number of 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrices with entries in {−1, 0, 1}?
cards.definition: Diagonal is 0; three free entries above it, each with 3 choices: 3³ = 27

cards.term: Trace of a square matrix: tr(A + B), tr(kA), tr(AB) vs tr(BA)?
cards.definition: tr A = sum of diagonal entries. tr(A + B) = tr A + tr B, tr(kA) = k tr A, and tr(AB) = tr(BA) (even if AB ≠ BA)

cards.term: If A and B are 3 × 3 with AB = BA, expand (A + B)³.
cards.definition: Only because they commute: A³ + 3A²B + 3AB² + B³. Same for (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² and A² − B² = (A − B)(A + B)

cards.term: If A² − A + I = O, what is A⁻¹?
cards.definition: Multiply A² − A + I = O by A⁻¹ (A is invertible, since A(A − I) = −I): A⁻¹ = I − A

cards.term: If A is a 3 × 3 matrix with A² = O, what is (I + A)⁻¹?
cards.definition: (I + A)(I − A) = I − A² = I, so (I + A)⁻¹ = I − A

cards.term:
MCQ: if a matrix has 12 elements, the number of possible orders is
(a) 4 (b) 6 (c) 8 (d) 12
cards.definition: Divisor pairs of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 → (b) 6

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is 3 × 4 and B is 4 × 2, the order of AB is
(a) 3 × 2 (b) 4 × 4 (c) 2 × 3 (d) not defined
cards.definition: (a) 3 × 2
Multiplying by B on the right swaps the columns: (a) [[2, 1], [4, 3]]

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is a square matrix with A² = A, then (I + A)² =
(a) I + A (b) I + 2A (c) I + 3A (d) I − A
cards.definition: I + 2A + A² = I + 3A: (c)

cards.term:
MCQ: if A = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], then A² =
(a) [[cos 2θ, −sin 2θ], [sin 2θ, cos 2θ]] (b) [[cos²θ, −sin²θ], [sin²θ, cos²θ]] (c) I (d) 2A
cards.definition: Rotation by θ twice is rotation by 2θ: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: the matrix [[0, 5, −7], [−5, 0, 11], [7, −11, 0]] is
(a) symmetric (b) skew-symmetric (c) diagonal (d) scalar
cards.definition: Zero diagonal and aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ: (b) skew-symmetric

cards.term:
MCQ: for a square matrix A, A + A′ is always
(a) skew-symmetric (b) symmetric (c) diagonal (d) identity
cards.definition: (b) symmetric

cards.term:
MCQ: if A is invertible, (A′)⁻¹ =
(a) A′ (b) (A⁻¹)′ (c) A (d) −A′
cards.definition: (b) (A⁻¹)′

cards.term:
MCQ: if A = [[1, 0], [0, −1]], then A² =
(a) A (b) −A (c) I (d) O
cards.definition: (c) I. A is involutory

cards.term:
MCQ: the number of 2 × 2 matrices with entries from {0, 1} is
(a) 4 (b) 8 (c) 16 (d) 2
cards.definition: 2⁴ = (c) 16

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): if A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], the (1, 2) entry of A¹⁰⁰ is?
cards.definition: Aⁿ = [[1, n], [0, 1]], so 100

cards.term: Integer answer: if A = [[2, 3], [1, 2]], the sum of the entries of A⁻¹ is?
cards.definition: ad − bc = 1, so A⁻¹ = [[2, −3], [−1, 2]]. Sum = 2 − 3 − 1 + 2 = 0

cards.term: Integer answer: how many 3 × 3 matrices with entries 0 or 1 are there with exactly two 1s?
cards.definition: Choose which 2 of 9 positions: ⁹C₂ = 36

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: if AB = O then A = O or B = O.
R: the product of two non-zero real numbers is non-zero.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A false, R true (d) Both false
cards.definition: (c): R is true for numbers, but matrices can be zero divisors: A = [[0, −1], [0, 2]], B = [[3, 5], [0, 0]] have AB = O

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: (AB)′ = A′B′ for all conformable A, B.
R: (AB)′ = B′A′.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: (b): the correct rule reverses the order, so A is false

cards.term: True/False: every diagonal matrix commutes with every square matrix of the same order.
cards.definition: False. Only scalar matrices commute with all matrices. diag(1, 2) does not commute with [[0, 1], [1, 0]]

cards.term: True/False: the product of two symmetric matrices is symmetric.
cards.definition: False in general; it is symmetric iff they commute

cards.term: 2-mark: if A = [[1, 2], [−1, 3]] find A′ and check (A′)′ = A.
3-mark: express [[2, 4], [1, 3]] as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
3-mark: A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]]. Show A² − 2A − 3I = O and hence find A⁻¹.
4-mark: if A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and f(x) = x² − 5x − 2, find f(A).
cards.definition: A² = [[7, 10], [15, 22]]; A² − 5A − 2I = [[7 − 5 − 2, 10 − 10], [15 − 15, 22 − 20 − 2]] = O (this is Cayley–Hamilton: tr A = 5, det A = −2)

cards.term: 4-mark: A = [[1, −1], [2, −1]], B = [[a, 1], [b, −1]] and (A + B)² = A² + B². Find a and b.
cards.definition: (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², so we need AB + BA = O. AB = [[a − b, 2], [2a − b, 3]] and BA = [[a + 2, −a − 1], [b − 2, 1 − b]]. Entry (1, 2): 2 − a − 1 = 0 gives a = 1; entry (1, 1): 2a − b + 2 = 0 gives b = 4. a = 1, b = 4

cards.term: Case-based: a shop sells pens, notebooks and files. Monday sales [30, 20, 10], price per item [₹5, ₹25, ₹40]. Write the revenue as a matrix product and compute it.
cards.definition: Row [30 20 10] times the column [5, 25, 40]ᵀ: 150 + 500 + 400 = ₹1050. A 1 × 3 times a 3 × 1 is 1 × 1

cards.term: Case-based: coordinates of triangle vertices are the columns of [[0, 4, 2], [0, 0, 3]]. Multiplying on the left by [[1, 0], [0, −1]] does what?
cards.definition: It changes the sign of every y-coordinate: reflection in the x-axis. New vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, −3)
